|  ![][image2] *They were told to start with 15 volts, then 30 volts, 45 volts, and so on, until they reached the maximum—a lethal dose of 450 volts. In reality, no electrical current was actually flowing; Milgram used an actor to play the role of the victim, but those charged with administering the shocks didn’t know that. The results were, well, shocking: As the person in the other room wailed and writhed in pain, and the subject administering the shock wanted to stop, the professor would say, “Keep going, the experiment depends on it.” The majority of people continued with the electrocution. More than half of the participants went all the way up to the maximum voltage—out of sheer obedience to authority.* Lack of information/conclusive evidence may lead to obismal decision making, which can cause a lot of harm in he longer run. |  ![][image2] *In the media, story bias rages like wildfire. For example: A car is driving over a bridge when the structure suddenly collapses. What do we read the next day? We hear the tale of the unlucky driver, where he came from, and where he was going. We read his biography: born somewhere, grew up somewhere else, earned a living as something. If he survives and can give interviews, we hear exactly how it felt when the bridge came crashing down. The absurd thing: Not one of these stories explains the underlying cause of the accident.* May 1, 2021 [44](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA44.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Suppose your region is experiencing a record period of cold weather. In all probability, the temperature will rise in the next few days—back toward the monthly average. The same goes for extreme heat, drought, or rain. Weather fluctuates around a mean. The same is true for chronic pain, golf handicaps, stock market performance, luck in love, subjective happiness, and test scores. In short, the crippling back pain would most likely have improved without a chiropractor. The handicap would have returned to 12 without additional lessons. And the performance of the investment adviser would also have shifted back toward the market average—with or without the restroom dance.* May 2, 2021 [61](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA61.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Say one million monkeys speculate on the stock market. They buy and sell stocks like crazy and, of course, completely at random. What happens? After one week, about half of the monkeys will have made a profit and the other half a loss. The ones that made a profit can stay; the ones that made a loss you send home. In the second week, one half of the monkeys will still be riding high, while the other half will have made a loss and are sent home. And so on. After ten weeks, about one thousand monkeys will be left—those who have always invested their money well. After twenty weeks, just one monkey will remain—this one always, without fail, chose the right stocks and is now a billionaire. Let’s call him the success monkey.* May 2, 2021 [63](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA63)  |
| ----- |

## *5: Why You Should Forget the Past: Sunk Cost Fallacy*

## *9: Don’t Bow to Authority: Authority Bias*

|  *![][image4] authority bias* Authority Bias \- Phenomenon where we tend to supress any decisions/evidence against the authority because of fear aroused from the power and status they hold April 27, 2021 [34](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA34.w.0.0.0.3)  |

The results were, well, shocking: As the person in the other room wailed and writhed in pain, and the subject administering the shock wanted to stop, the professor would say, “Keep going, the experiment depends on it.” The majority of people continued with the electrocution. More than half of the participants went all the way up to the maximum voltage—out of sheer obedience to authority.* Lack of information/conclusive evidence may lead to obismal decision making, which can cause a lot of harm in he longer run. ## *10: Leave Your Supermodel Friends at Home: Contrast Effect*

|  *![][image4] contrast effect* Contrast Effect \- The effect of something rises deeply if we are subjected to much worse than if we were to see the "something" normally. April 27, 2021 [36](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA36.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *We judge something to be beautiful, expensive, or large if we have something ugly, cheap, or small in front of us. | ----- |

|  ![][image2] *The contrast effect is at work in other places, too. Experiments show that people are willing to walk an extra ten minutes to save \$10 on food. Logically, you should walk back in both cases or not at all.* April 27, 2021 [36](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA36.w.0.0.0.4)  |

## *13: Even True Stories Are Fairy Tales: Story Bias*

|  *![][image5] Even True Stories Are Fairy Tales* May 1, 2021 [44](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA44)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *Here, we speak about “understanding,” but these things cannot be understood in the traditional sense* May 1, 2021 [44](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA44.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *We simply build the meaning into them afterward* May 1, 2021 [44](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA44.w.0.0.0.3)  |

|  ![][image5] *Stories are dubious entities. They simplify and distort reality and filter things that don’t fit. But apparently we cannot do without them. Why remains unclear* May 1, 2021 [44](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA44.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *In the media, story bias rages like wildfire. For example: A car is driving over a bridge when the structure suddenly collapses. What do we read the next day? We hear the tale of the unlucky driver, where he came from, and where he was going. We read his biography: born somewhere, grew up somewhere else, earned a living as something. If he survives and can give interviews, we hear exactly how it felt when the bridge came crashing down. The absurd thing: Not one of these stories explains the underlying cause of the accident.* May 1, 2021 [44](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA44.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *Stories attract us; abstract details repel us. Consequently, entertaining side issues and backstories are prioritized over relevant facts. | ----- |

|  ![][image3] *Advertisers have learned to capitalize on this, too. Instead of focusing on an item’s benefits, they create a story around it.* May 1, 2021 [45](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA45.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *you’ll see that your life has not followed a straight line leading to today, but has been a series of unplanned, unconnected events and* May 1, 2021 [46](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA46)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *experiences* May 1, 2021 [46](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA46)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *The real issue with stories: They give us a false sense of understanding, which inevitably leads us to take bigger risks and urges us to take a stroll on thin ice.* May 1, 2021 [46](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA46.w.0.0.0.1)  |

We can aptly describe it as the “I told you so” phenomenon: In retrospect, everything seems clear and inevitable.* May 1, 2021 [47](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA47.w.0.0.0.3)  |

## *15: Why You Systematically Overestimate Your Knowledge and Abilities: Overconfidence Effect*

|  *![][image3] The overconfidence effect also applies to forecasts, such as stock market performance over a year or your firm’s profits over three years. We systematically overestimate our knowledge and our ability to predict—on a massive scale.* May 1, 2021 [49](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA49.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *The overconfidence effect does not deal with whether single estimates are correct or not. Rather, it measures the difference between what people really know and what they think they know. What’s surprising is this: Experts suffer even more from the overconfidence effect than laypeople do.* May 1, 2021 [49](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA49.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *Why is that? Here, two effects act in unison. First, you have the classic overconfidence effect. Second, those with a direct interest in the project have an incentive to underestimate the costs: Consultants, contractors, and suppliers seek follow-up orders* May 1, 2021 [50](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA50.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *What makes the overconfidence effect so prevalent and its effect so confounding is that it is not driven by incentives; it is raw and innate. And it’s not counterbalanced by the opposite effect, “underconfidence,” which doesn’t exist* May 1, 2021 [50](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA50.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *In conclusion: Be aware that you tend to overestimate your knowledge. Be skeptical of predictions, especially if they come from so-called experts. And with all plans, favor the pessimistic scenario. This way, you have a chance of judging the situation somewhat realistically.* May 1, 2021 [51](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA51)  |
| ----- |

## *16: Don’t Take News Anchors Seriously: Chauffeur Knowledge*

|  *![][image3] there are two types of knowledge. First, we have real knowledge. We see it in people who have committed a large amount of time and effort to understanding a topic. The second type is chauffeur knowledge—knowledge from people who have learned to put on a show. Maybe they have a great voice or good hair, but the knowledge they espouse is not their own. They reel off eloquent words as if reading from a script.* May 1, 2021 [52](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA52.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *With news anchors, however, it is still easy. These are actors. Period. Everyone knows it. And yet it continues to astound me how much respect these perfectly coiffed script readers enjoy, not to mention how much they earn, moderating panels about topics they barely fathom.* May 1, 2021 [52](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA52.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Munger underscores this: “So you have to figure out what your own aptitudes are. If you play games where other people have the aptitudes and you don’t, you’re going to lose. And that’s as close to certain as any prediction that you can make. You have to figure out where you’ve got an edge. And you’ve got to play within your own circle of competence.”* May 1, 2021 [53](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA53.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *True experts recognize the limits of what they know and what they do not know. If they find themselves outside their circle of competence, they keep quiet or simply say, “I don’t know.” This they utter unapologetically, even with a certain pride. From chauffeurs, we hear every line except this.* May 1, 2021 [53](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA53.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

## *18: Never Pay Your Lawyer by the Hour: Incentive Super-Response Tendency*

|  *![][image3] People respond to incentives by doing what is in their best interests. What is noteworthy is, first, how quickly and radically people’s behavior changes when incentives come into play or are altered, and second, the fact that people respond to the incentives themselves, and not the grander intentions behind them.* May 1, 2021 [58](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA58.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *Good incentive systems comprise both intent and reward. An example: In ancient Rome, engineers were made to stand underneath the construction at their bridges’ opening ceremonies. Poor incentive systems, on the other hand, overlook and sometimes even pervert the underlying aim.* May 1, 2021 [58](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA58.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *And then it came to me: The answer lies in incentive systems. If they came back alive, they could keep the spoils of war and live out their days as rich men. If they died, they automatically passed on to the afterlife as martyrs—with all the benefits that came with it. It was win-win* May 1, 2021 [59](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA59.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *Be wary, too, of investment advisers endorsing particular financial products. They are not interested in your financial well-being, but in earning a commission on these products. The same goes for entrepreneurs’ and investment bankers’ business plans. These are often worthless because, again, the vendors have their own interests at heart. What is the old adage? “Never ask a barber if you need a haircut.”* May 1, 2021 [59](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA59.w.0.0.0.3)  |

## *19: The Dubious Efficacy of Doctors, Consultants, and Psychotherapists: Regression to Mean*

|  *![][image4] His back pain was sometimes better, sometimes worse. There were days when he felt like he could move mountains, and those when he could barely move.* May 2, 2021 [61](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA61)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *What links the three men is a fallacy: the regression-to-mean delusion.* May 2, 2021 [61](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA61.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Suppose your region is experiencing a record period of cold weather. In all probability, the temperature will rise in the next few days—back toward the monthly average. The same goes for extreme heat, drought, or rain. Weather fluctuates around a mean. The same is true for chronic pain, golf handicaps, stock market performance, luck in love, subjective happiness, and test scores. In short, the crippling back pain would most likely have improved without a chiropractor. The handicap would have returned to 12 without additional lessons. And the performance of the investment adviser would also have shifted back toward the market average—with or without the restroom dance.* May 2, 2021 [61](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA61.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *Ignoring regression to mean can have destructive consequences, such as teachers (or managers) concluding that the stick is better than the carrot. For example, following a test, the highest-performing students are praised and the lowest are castigated.* May 2, 2021 [62](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA62.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *look out for our old friend, the regression-to-mean error.* May 2, 2021 [62](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA62.w.0.0.0.4)  |

## *20: Never Judge a Decision by Its Outcome: Outcome Bias*

|  *![][image2] Say one million monkeys speculate on the stock market. They buy and sell stocks like crazy and, of course, completely at random. What happens? After one week, about half of the monkeys will have made a profit and the other half a loss. The ones that made a profit can stay; the ones that made a loss you send home. In the second week, one half of the monkeys will still be riding high, while the other half will have made a loss and are sent home. And so on. After ten weeks, about one thousand monkeys will be left—those who have always invested their money well. After twenty weeks, just one monkey will remain—this one always, without fail, chose the right stocks and is now a billionaire. Let’s call him the success monkey.* May 2, 2021 [63](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA63)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *How does the media react? It will pounce on this animal* May 2, 2021 [63](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA63.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *to understand its “success principles.” And they will find some: Perhaps the monkey eats more bananas than the others. Perhaps he sits in another corner of the cage. Or maybe he swings headlong through the branches, or he takes long, reflective pauses while grooming. He must have some recipe for success, right? How else could he perform so brilliantly? Spot-on for two years—and that from a simple monkey? Impossible\!* May 2, 2021 [63](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA63.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *The monkey story illustrates the outcome bias: We tend to evaluate decisions based on the result rather than on the decision process. This fallacy is also known as the “historian error.”* May 2, 2021 [63](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA63.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *To assess the quality of the decision, we must use the information available at the time, filtering out everything we know about it postattack* May 2, 2021 [63](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA63.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *In other words, you assess the process and not the result.* May 2, 2021 [64](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA64.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *In conclusion: Never judge a decision purely by its result, especially when randomness and “external factors” play a role. A bad result does not automatically indicate a bad decision and vice versa.* May 2, 2021 [64](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA64.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

## *21: Less Is More: Paradox of Choice*

|  *![][image5] Nowadays, people are bombarded with options, such as hundreds of mental disorders, thousands* May 2, 2021 [66](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA66.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *of different careers, even more holiday destinations, and an infinite variety of lifestyles. There has never been more choice.* May 2, 2021 [66](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA66.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *And yet selection is the yardstick of progress. It is what sets us apart from planned economies and the Stone Age. Yes, abundance makes you giddy, but there is a limit. When it is exceeded, a surfeit of choices destroys quality of life. The technical term for this is the paradox of choice* May 2, 2021 [66](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA66.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Second, a broader selection leads to poorer decisions. If you ask young people what is important in a life partner,* May 2, 2021 [67](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA67.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *they reel off all the usual qualities: intelligence, good manners, warmth, the ability to listen, a sense of humor, and physical attractiveness. But do they actually take these criteria into account when choosing someone?* May 2, 2021 [67](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA67.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *It has been proven that the stress caused by this mind-boggling variety is so large that the male brain reduces the decision to one single criterion: physical attractiveness.* May 2, 2021 [67](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA67.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *Finally, large selection leads to discontent. How can you be sure you are making the right choice when two hundred options surround and confound you? The answer is: You cannot. The more choice you have, the more unsure and therefore dissatisfied you are afterward.* May 2, 2021 [67](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA67.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *In this age of unlimited variety, rather the opposite is true: “Good enough” is the new optimum* May 2, 2021 [68](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA68)  |

## *22: You Like Me, You Really, Really Like Me: Liking Bias*

|  *![][image3] The liking bias is startlingly simple to understand and yet we continually fall prey to it. It means this: The more we like someone, the more inclined we are to buy from or help that person.* May 2, 2021 [69](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA69.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *According to research, we see people as pleasant, if (a) they are outwardly attractive, (b) they are similar to us in terms of origin, personality, or interests, and (c) they like us. Consequently, advertising is full of attractive people. Ugly people seem unfriendly and don’t even make it into the background (see A). In addition to engaging super-attractive types, advertising also employs “people like you and me” (see B)—those who are similar in appearance, accent, or background. In short, the more similar, the better.* May 2, 2021 [69](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA69.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *How many times have you bought something “because you’re worth it”? Here factor C comes into play: We find people appealing if they like us. Compliments work wonders, even if they ring hollow as a drum.* May 2, 2021 [69](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA69.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Conservation organizations also carefully select who gets the starring role in their advertisements. Have you ever seen a World Wildlife Fund brochure filled with spiders, worms, algae, or bacteria? They are perhaps just as endangered as pandas, gorillas, koalas, and seals—and even more important for the ecosystem.* May 2, 2021 [70](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA70.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Politicians, too, are maestros of the liking bias. Depending on the makeup and interests of an audience, they emphasize different topics, such as residential area, social background, or economic issues. And they flatter us:* May 2, 2021 [70](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA70.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *Amiability works better than bribery.”* May 2, 2021 [71](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA71)  |

## *23: Don’t Cling to Things: Endowment Effect*

|  *![][image3] the endowment effect. We consider things to be more valuable the moment we own them. In other words, if we are selling something, we charge more for it than what we ourselves would be willing to spend.* May 2, 2021 [72](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA72.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *We consider things to be more valuable the moment we own them. In other words, if we are selling something, we charge more for it than what we ourselves would be willing to spend.* May 2, 2021 [72](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA72.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *In real estate, the endowment effect is palpable. Sellers become emotionally attached to their houses and thus systematically overestimate their value. They balk at the market price, expecting buyers to pay more—which is completely absurd since this excess is little more than sentimental value* May 2, 2021 [72](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA72.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *Don’t cling to things. Consider your property something that the “universe” (whatever you believe this to be) has bestowed to you temporarily. Keep in mind that it can recoup this (or more) in the blink of an eye.* May 2, 2021 [73](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA73.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *We can safely say that we are better at collecting things than at casting them off. Not only does this explain why we fill our homes with junk, but also why lovers of stamps, watches, and pieces of art part with them so seldomly.* May 2, 2021 [74](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA74.w.0.0.0.1.0.1)  |

## *25: The Calamity of Conformity: Groupthink*

|  *![][image3] Moreover, you might not be 100 percent sure why you disagree, whereas the others are unanimous—and far from stupid. So you keep your mouth shut for another day. When everyone thinks and acts like this, groupthink is at work* May 5, 2021 [78](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA78)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *This is where a group of smart people makes reckless decisions because everyone aligns their opinions with the supposed consensus.* May 5, 2021 [78](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA78.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Next comes the illusion of unanimity: If the others are of the same opinion, any dissenting view must be wrong. No one wants to be the naysayer that destroys team unity. Finally, each person is happy to be part of the group. Expressing reservations could mean exclusion from it.* May 5, 2021 [79](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA79.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *If you ever find yourself in a tight, unanimous group, you must speak your mind, even if your team does not like it. Question tacit assumptions, even if you risk expulsion from the warm nest. And, if you lead a group, appoint someone as devil’s advocate. She will not be the most popular member of the team, but she might be the most important.* May 5, 2021 [79](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA79.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Members of a close-knit group cultivate team spirit by (unconsciously) building illusions.* May 5, 2021 [80](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA80.w.0.0.0.1.0.1)  |

## *26: Why You’ll Soon Be Playing Mega Trillions: Neglect of Probability*

|  *![][image4] Our emotions draw us to the first game, even though the second is ten times better, objectively considered (expected win times probability). Therefore, the trend is toward ever-larger jackpots—Mega Millions, Mega Billions, Mega Trillions—no matter how small the odds are.* May 5, 2021 [81](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA81.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *We lack an intuitive grasp of probability.* May 5, 2021 [81](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA81.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *The proper term for this is neglect of probability, and it leads to errors in decision making. We invest in start-ups because the potential profit makes dollar signs flash before our eyes, but we forget (or are too lazy) to investigate the slim chances of new businesses actually achieving such growth.* May 5, 2021 [81](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA81.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *If you think like most people, you will opt for method B—which is silly because with measure A, 3 percent fewer people die, and with B, just 1 percent fewer. Method A is three times as good\! This fallacy is called the “zero-risk bias.”* May 5, 2021 [82](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA82.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *We have no intuitive grasp of risk and thus distinguish poorly among different threats. The more serious the threat and the more emotional the topic (such as radioactivity), the less reassuring a reduction in risk seems to us* May 5, 2021 [83](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA83.w.0.0.0.1)  |

## *27: Why the Last Cookie in the Jar Makes Your Mouth Water: Scarcity Error*

|  *![][image3] Rara sunt cara, said the Romans. Rare is valuable. In fact, the scarcity error is as old as mankind.* May 5, 2021 [84](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA84.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *Gallery owners take advantage of the scarcity error by placing red “sold” dots under most of their paintings, transforming the remaining few works into rare items that must be snatched up quickly.* May 5, 2021 [85](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA85.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image2] *The poster that was no longer available was suddenly classified as the most beautiful. In psychology, this phenomenon is called “reactance”: When we are deprived of an option, we suddenly deem it more attractive. It is a kind of act of defiance. It is also known as the “Romeo and Juliet effect”: Because the love between the tragic Shakespearean teenagers is forbidden, it knows no bounds* May 5, 2021 [85](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA85.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *In conclusion: The typical response to scarcity is a lapse in clear thinking. Assess products and services solely on the basis of their price and benefits.* May 5, 2021 [86](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA86)  |

## *28: When You Hear Hoofbeats, Don’t Expect a Zebra: Base-Rate Neglect*

|  *![][image2] Mark is a thin man from Germany with glasses who likes to listen to Mozart. Which is more likely? That (a) Mark is a truck driver or (b) he is a professor of literature in Frankfurt. Most will bet on B, which is wrong. Germany has ten thousand times more truck drivers than Frankfurt has literature professors* May 5, 2021 [87](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA87)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *The detailed description enticed us to overlook the statistical reality. Scientists call this fallacy base-rate neglect: a disregard of fundamental distribution levels. It is one of the most common errors in reasoning. Virtually all journalists, economists, and politicians fall for it on a regular basis* May 5, 2021 [87](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA87.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *This is very reasonable. In medical school, residents spend a lot of time purging base-rate neglect. The motto drummed into any prospective doctor in the United States is: “When you hear hoofbeats behind you, don’t expect to see a zebra,” which means: Investigate the most likely ailments before you start diagnosing exotic diseases, even if you are a specialist in that* May 5, 2021 [87](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA87.w.0.0.0.3)  |

## *32: Why Evil Is More Striking Than Good: Loss Aversion*

|  *![][image3] loss “weighs” about twice that of a similar gain. Social scientists call this loss aversion* May 7, 2021 [99](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA99.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *For this reason, if you want to convince someone about something, don’t focus on the advantages; instead highlight how it helps them dodge the disadvantages* May 7, 2021 [99](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA99.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *The fear of losing something motivates people more than the prospect of gaining something of equal value.* May 7, 2021 [100](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA100)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *Why risk something that brings them, at best, a nice bonus, and at worst, a pink slip? The downside is larger than the upside. In almost all companies and situations, safeguarding your career trumps any potential reward.* May 7, 2021 [100](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA100.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *We can’t fight it: Evil is more powerful and more plentiful than good. We are more sensitive to negative than to positive things. On the street, scary faces stand out more than smiling ones. ## *33: Why Teams Are Lazy: Social Loafing*

|  *![][image3] Science calls this the social loafing effect. It occurs when individual performance is not directly visible; it blends into the group effort.* May 7, 2021 [102](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA102.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *Social loafing is rational behavior: Why invest all of your* May 7, 2021 [102](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA102.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *energy when half will do—especially when this little shortcut goes unnoticed? Quite simply, social loafing is a form of cheating of which we are all guilty even if it takes place unconsciously, just as it does with the horses.* May 7, 2021 [102](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA102.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *When people work together, individual performances decrease. This isn’t surprising. What is noteworthy, however, is that our input doesn’t grind to a complete halt* May 7, 2021 [102](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA102.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *Social loafing does not occur solely in physical performance. We slack off mentally, too. For example, in meetings, the larger the team, the weaker our individual participation. However, once a certain number of participants are involved, our performance plateaus.* May 7, 2021 [102](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA102.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *Social loafing has interesting implications. In groups, we tend to hold back not only in terms of participation but also in terms of accountability.* May 7, 2021 [103](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA103.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *We hide behind team decisions. The technical term for this is “diffusion of responsibility.” For the same reason, teams tend to take bigger risks than their members would take on their own.* May 7, 2021 [103](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA103.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *In conclusion: People behave differently in groups than when alone (otherwise there would be no groups). The disadvantages of groups can be mitigated by making individual performances as visible as possible. Long live meritocracy\! Long live the performance society\!* May 7, 2021 [103](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA103.w.0.0.0.4)  |

## *37: Why You Shouldn’t Believe in the Stork: False Causality*

|  *![][image3] false causality* It acts like the prosecutor's fallacy or third cause fallacy. Prosecutor's fallacy states that if A causes B, then B is the cause of A, which is not true in most cases. Third cause fallacy states that people tend to relate two unrelated situations to each other, even though they may not have a common link, but an entirely different third link, which causes the two. May 10, 2021 [113](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA113.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *In conclusion: Correlation is not causality. Take a closer look at linked events: Sometimes what is presented as the cause turns out to be the effect, and vice versa. And sometimes there is no link at all* May 10, 2021 [113](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA113.w.0.0.0.4)  |

## *38: Why Attractive People Climb the Career Ladder More Quickly: Halo Effect*

|  *![][image4] The halo effect occurs when a single aspect dazzles us and affects how we see the full picture. In the case of Cisco, its halo shone particularly bright. Journalists were astounded by its stock prices and assumed the entire business was just as brilliant—without closer investigation* May 10, 2021 [115](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA115.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *We often ascribe success and superiority where little is due, such as when we favor products from a manufacturer simply because of its good reputation* May 10, 2021 [115](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA115.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *The psychologist Edward Lee Thorndike discovered the halo effect nearly one hundred years ago. His conclusion was that a single quality (e.g., beauty, social status, age) produces a positive or negative impression that outshines everything else, and the overall effect is disproportionate.* May 10, 2021 [115](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA115.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *We are so used to seeing celebrities promoting arbitrary products that we never stop to consider why their support should be of any importance to us. But this is exactly the sneaky part of the halo effect: It works on a subconscious level. All that needs to register is the attractive face, dream lifestyle—and that product* May 10, 2021 [116](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA116.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *The halo effect obstructs our view of true characteristics. To counteract this, go beyond face value. Factor out the most striking features.* May 10, 2021 [116](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA116.w.0.0.0.4)  |

## *41: The Deception of Specific Cases: Conjunction Fallacy*

|  *![][image4] The conjunction fallacy is at play when such a subset seems larger than the entire set—which by definition cannot be the case.* May 10, 2021 [123](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA123.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *We are easy prey for the conjunction fallacy because we have an innate attraction to “harmonious” or “plausible” stories. The more convincingly, impressively, or vividly that Chris the aid worker is portrayed, the greater the risk of false reasoning.* May 10, 2021 [123](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA123.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *Kahneman believes that two types of thinking exist: The first kind is intuitive, automatic, and direct. The second is conscious, rational, slow, laborious, and logical. Unfortunately, intuitive thinking draws conclusions long before the conscious mind does.* May 10, 2021 [124](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA124.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *In conclusion: Forget about left brains and right brains: The difference between intuitive and conscious thinking is much more significant. With important decisions, remember that, at the intuitive level, we have a soft spot for plausible stories. Therefore, be on the lookout for convenient details and happy endings. Remember: If an additional condition has to be met, no matter how plausible it sounds, it will become less, not more, likely.* May 10, 2021 [124](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA124.w.0.0.0.3)  |

## *64: How to Expose a Charlatan: Forer Effect*

|  *![][image5] “You have a great need for other people to like and admire you. You have a tendency to be critical of yourself. You have a great deal of unused capacity, which you have not turned to your advantage. While you have some personality weaknesses, you are generally able to compensate for them. Your sexual adjustment has presented problems for you. Disciplined and self-controlled outside, you tend to be worrisome and insecure inside. At times you have serious doubts as to whether you have made the right decision or done the right thing. You prefer a certain amount of change and variety and become dissatisfied when hemmed in by restrictions and limitations. You pride yourself as an independent thinker and do not accept others’ statements without* July 5, 2021 [186](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA186)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *satisfactory proof. You have found it unwise to be too frank in revealing yourself to others. At times you are extroverted, affable, and sociable while at other times you are introverted, wary, and reserved. Some of your aspirations tend to be pretty unrealistic. Security is one of your major goals in life.”* July 5, 2021 [186](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA186.w.0.0.0.2)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *People tend to identify many of their own traits in such universal descriptions* July 5, 2021 [186](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA186.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *What’s behind the Forer effect? First, the majority of statements in Forer’s passage are so general that they relate to everyone: “Sometimes you seriously doubt your actions.”* July 5, 2021 [187](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA187)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *Who doesn’t? Second, we tend to accept flattering statements that don’t apply to us: “You are proud of your independent thinking.” Obviously\! Who sees himself or herself as a mindless follower?* July 5, 2021 [187](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA187)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *positive effect plays a part: The text contains no negative statements; it states only what we are, even though the absence of characteristics is an equally important part of a person’s makeup.* July 5, 2021 [187](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA187.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *Fourth, the father of all the fallacies, the confirmation bias: We accept whatever corresponds to our self-image and unconsciously filter everything else out. What remains is a coherent portrait.* July 5, 2021 [187](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA187.w.0.0.0.1)  |

## *66: Why You Are a Slave to Your Emotions: Affect Heuristic*

|  *![][image4] We are limited by what springs to mind; we can only conjure up what we have seen in our modest experience* July 5, 2021 [191](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA191.w.0.0.0.3)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image4] *In our evolutionary past, whoever thought too long and hard vanished inside a predator’s jaws. We are the descendants of quick decision makers, and we rely on mental shortcuts called heuristics* July 5, 2021 [191](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA191.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *One of the most popular is the affect heuristic. An affect is a momentary judgment: something you like or dislike. The word “gunfire” triggers a negative effect. The word “luxury” produces a positive one. This automatic, one-dimensional impulse prevents you from considering risks and benefits to be independent variables, which indeed they are* July 5, 2021 [192](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA192)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image3] *Instead, the affect heuristic puts risks and benefits on the same sensory thread* July 5, 2021 [192](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA192)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *like something, you believe that the risks are smaller and the benefits greater than they actually are. If you don’t like something, the opposite is true. Risks and benefits appear to be dependent. Of course, in reality, they are not.* July 5, 2021 [192](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA192.w.0.0.0.1)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *Whether we like it or not, we are puppets of our* July 5, 2021 [193](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA193)  |
| ----- |

|  ![][image5] *emotions. We make complex decisions by consulting our feelings, not our thoughts. Against our best intentions, we substitute the question, “What do I think about this?” with “How do I feel about this?” So, smile\! Your future depends on it.* July 5, 2021 [193](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA193)  |

|  ![][image4] *To rebuff an anecdote is difficult because it is a mini-story, and we know how vulnerable our brains are to those* July 20, 2021 [268](http://play.google.com/books/reader?printsec=frontcover&output=reader&id=hhNZKgAAAEAJ&source=books-notes-export&pg=GBS.PA268.w.0.0.0.4)  |
| ----- |

## *97: The Stone Age Hunt for Scapegoats: Fallacy of the Single Cause*

|  *![][image4] Rather, there are hundreds, thousands, an infinite number of factors that add up.
